slides.title: Welcome to Nuclear Reactions
slides.content:
# Nuclear Reactions

Welcome to the module on **Nuclear Reactions**.

## What You Will Learn:
- **Reaction mechanisms** - How nuclei interact
- **Cross-section measurements** - The probability of a reaction
- **Nuclear astrophysics** - Powering the stars
- **Synthesis processes** - How the elements were made

Nuclear reactions are the engines of the universe, responsible for all the elements heavier than lithium.

slides.title: Reaction Mechanisms
slides.content:
# Reaction Mechanisms

A nuclear reaction occurs when a projectile (like a proton, neutron, or another nucleus) hits a target nucleus.

## Two Extremes of Reactions:
1. **Direct Reactions:** The projectile grazes the target, knocking out or transferring just one or two nucleons in a fraction of a second.
2. **Compound Nucleus Reactions:** The projectile crashes head-on, completely merging with the target to form a highly excited, boiling "compound nucleus" that later decays.

slides.title: Fission vs Fusion
slides.content:
# Fission and Fusion

The two most famous nuclear reactions release immense amounts of energy.

## Fission:
A heavy nucleus (like Uranium) splits into two lighter fragments. This releases energy because the fragments are more tightly bound. This powers nuclear reactors.

## Fusion:
Two light nuclei (like Hydrogen) smash together and merge into a heavier nucleus (Helium). This powers the sun and hydrogen bombs.

slides.title: The Coulomb Barrier
slides.content:
# The Coulomb Barrier

Why don't nuclei undergo fusion all the time?

## Electrostatic Repulsion:
Because all nuclei are positively charged, they repel each other fiercely. This repulsive force creates a massive energy wall known as the **Coulomb Barrier**.

To achieve fusion, nuclei must be hurled at each other at incredible speeds (requiring temperatures of millions of degrees) to overcome this barrier and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to take over.

slides.title: Cross-Section Measurements
slides.content:
# Cross-Section Measurements

In nuclear physics, we measure the probability that a specific reaction will occur using the concept of a **Cross-Section**.

## The Target Area:
Imagine throwing darts at a wall. The cross-section is the effective "size" of the target bullseye. 

- A large cross-section means the reaction is highly probable.
- A small cross-section means the reaction is rare.

slides.title: Reactions Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of basic reaction types.
slides.quizQuestion: What force creates the massive barrier that prevents light nuclei from easily undergoing fusion at room temperature?

slides.title: The Barn Unit
slides.content:
# The Barn

Nuclear cross-sections are measured in a unit whimsically called the **Barn**.

## The Origin:
During the Manhattan Project, physicists described a uranium nucleus as being "as big as a barn" for a slow-moving neutron to hit.

**1 Barn = 10^-28 square meters.** 

It is an unimaginably small area to us, but for a neutron, it is a massive, easy-to-hit target!

slides.title: Resonances
slides.content:
# Nuclear Resonances

Cross-sections are not constant; they depend heavily on the energy of the incoming projectile.

## Excitation Functions:
If you plot the cross-section against the energy of the incoming particle, you often see massive spikes called **Resonances**.

This happens when the energy of the projectile perfectly matches a natural quantum vibration frequency of the target nucleus, dramatically increasing the probability of absorption.

slides.title: Nuclear Astrophysics
slides.content:
# Nuclear Astrophysics

Nuclear Astrophysics is the study of how nuclear reactions power the stars and synthesize the elements of the periodic table.

## The Big Bang:
The Big Bang only created three elements: Hydrogen, Helium, and a tiny trace of Lithium.

Every single other element in your body—the carbon in your DNA, the iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones—was forged in the crushing heat of a star!

slides.title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
slides.content:
# Stellar Nucleosynthesis

Stars are essentially giant, floating nuclear fusion reactors.

## The p-p Chain:
In stars like our Sun, the core temperature is about 15 million degrees. The primary reaction is the **proton-proton (p-p) chain**, which slowly fuses four single protons (hydrogen) into one helium nucleus, releasing energy that keeps the star from collapsing under its own gravity.

slides.title: The CNO Cycle
slides.content:
# The CNO Cycle

In stars much heavier and hotter than our Sun, hydrogen fusion occurs via a different mechanism: the **CNO Cycle**.

## Catalytic Fusion:
Carbon, Nitrogen, and Oxygen act as catalysts. They capture protons in a loop, eventually spitting out a Helium nucleus and regenerating the original Carbon.

This cycle is incredibly sensitive to temperature and runs much faster than the p-p chain, which is why massive stars burn out and die much quicker than small stars.

slides.title: Astrophysics Quiz
slides.content: Verify your knowledge of stellar fusion.
slides.quizQuestion: Which elements were the only ones created directly by the Big Bang?

slides.title: Synthesis of Heavy Elements
slides.content:
# Synthesis Processes

Stars can fuse elements up to Iron. Iron has the highest binding energy per nucleon; fusing it actually *consumes* energy instead of releasing it.

So how do we get gold, lead, and uranium?

## Neutron Capture:
Heavy elements are built via neutron capture. Because neutrons have no charge, they ignore the Coulomb barrier and easily slip into heavy nuclei, building them up step by step.

slides.title: The s-Process and r-Process
slides.content:
# Slow and Rapid Neutron Capture

## The s-Process (Slow):
Occurs inside dying red giant stars. Neutrons are captured slowly over thousands of years. This allows unstable nuclei time to undergo beta decay before capturing another neutron. This process creates about half of the elements heavier than iron.

## The r-Process (Rapid):
Occurs in violent cosmic explosions, like supernovas or colliding neutron stars. Nuclei are bombarded by billions of neutrons in less than a second! This creates the heaviest elements like Gold and Uranium.

slides.title: Superheavy Elements
slides.content:
# Synthesizing Superheavy Elements

The heaviest elements on the periodic table (like Oganesson, element 118) do not exist in nature. They must be synthesized in laboratories.

## Cold and Hot Fusion:
Physicists use particle accelerators to smash heavy ion beams (like Calcium-48) into ultra-heavy targets (like Californium). 

If the stars align perfectly, they overcome the Coulomb barrier and fuse into a superheavy element, which usually decays in a fraction of a millisecond.

slides.title: Summary of Nuclear Reactions
slides.content:
# Reactions Summary

## Key Takeaways:
- Reactions require overcoming the **Coulomb Barrier**.
- Reaction probabilities are measured in **Barns** (cross-sections), which spike wildly at certain energy **Resonances**.
- **Stellar nucleosynthesis** powers stars via the p-p chain and CNO cycle.
- Heavy elements are forged by the **s-process** (in red giants) and the **r-process** (in supernovas and neutron star collisions).
- **Superheavy elements** are artificially created in lab accelerators.
